text: [1:30]  Recap Bora's proposition for anyone not close to it: one calibrated velocity pulse instead of a 90 s record, amplitude set by a spectral match, re-calibrated at the softened period after every run. LAND THIS: the ~10x cost saving is the entire reason the surrogate exists and nothing today challenges it. Then be generous about what IMC2026 genuinely established - stiffness, period elongation, mechanism, damage pattern. You need the room to accept the diagnosis later, so establish first that you are not attacking the method.

text: [2:00]  THE PIVOT SLIDE. Two runs, different records, different scale factors, the same ratio to 1%. The model returns what it is handed to within 15%. Therefore the deficit sits upstream of the contact model, the block kinematics and the damping - none of those can be the cause if the model is already delivering its instruction faithfully. WEAKEST LINK: only run 21 is fully clean. FR76's input calibration is off by ~1.3x because Table 2's PTA is a four-specimen average. If pushed, lead with run 21 and concede run 24 carries that uncertainty. Land the consequence: if the model returns approximately Sd_target linearly, the IDA is not measuring nonlinear capacity - it is redrawing the input spectrum.

text: [1:30]  Orientation slide - keep it quick. Three records, escalating multipliers, EC40 interleaved as low-amplitude damage checks. Two things to land: (1) the protocol is fixed by the experiment - we reproduce it, we do not redesign it; (2) the run-21 to run-22 transition - HU12 at 600% gives 17 mm, FR76 at 100% gives less, then 175% gives 29.5 mm. name: Text 5
text: Housner is a free-standing block.  Ours is held at the top, pressed by springs and tied to joists. It gives 0.68 s where the measurements say 0.26–0.35 s.
textPreview: Housner is a free-standing block.  Ours is held at the top, pressed by springs and tied to joists. It gives 0.68 s where the measurements...

text: [2:00]  Explain the curve in one line: a rocking block has no fixed period - the further it leans, the slower it rocks, because the weight has less lever arm to push it back. That is the physics we are using, and the idea is sound. The problem is the formula. Housner assumes a free block; ours is restrained at the top, precompressed and tied to joists. Two independent checks say the period at 30 mm is 0.26-0.35 s, not 0.68 s. And Housner puts overturning at 208 mm while the test never went past 30 mm - so it would say the wall was nowhere near failure. Land this: keep the idea, replace the formula with a secant period from a pushover.

text: [2:00]  Show the result honestly. The curve crosses the experiment at run 24, but the log says runs 22-25 were driven at 0.87, 1.20, 1.67 and 2.80 g against a table that reached 0.78 g, and the cycle count hit its code limit of 10 on all four. So run 24 is not a prediction of 29.5 mm - the driver commanded 65.5 mm of spectral displacement and the model returned 32. The fix is one variable: shape the pulse at the rocking period rather than only reading Sd there. That gives the same demand at 0.30-0.57 g, all inside table capacity, and the commanded values then land within 5-11 percent of what the table actually applied. That last point is the result worth showing - the scheme finds the right intensity on its own.

text: [2:00]  This is the answer to question 1, and it splits. With the measured table motion and nothing adaptive at all, the model tracks the experiment through run 22 - including the dip at the record switch, which no pulse variant reproduced because it is a property of the record, not the intensity. So the under-prediction we have argued about all along was the LOADING for runs 1-22. But runs 23 and 24 stay short by 2.2x and 3.6x under the real record - there is no loading left to blame, so that residual is the MODEL. Candidates in order: small strain (this run had it off, and rocking softening is geometric), the bonded joist pockets, the rigid-block toe. Run 25 reaching 41.6 mm shows the model can go large - it gets there one run late, which reads as damage accumulating too slowly. One bookkeeping note: runs 1-6 report exactly zero while Ch4 alone reads about 2 mm - likely an export or averaging artefact, being checked.

text: [1:30]  Period, right panel: the elongation curves end at the same place, 1.18 for both. The model starts 8 percent high in absolute terms (0.0985 vs 0.091 s) but accumulates damage at the right rate. Tilt, left: peak tilt tracks the experiment to run 21 and reproduces the run-22 dip. Tilt, right: the one clear miss - both walls lean steadily from run 1 (that is the joist slip, 8-12 mm cumulative in the paper) while the model holds zero until run 18. With the pockets bonded, the model has no mechanism for that early drift. It catches the late positive swing though, and ends near the measured value.

text: [1:30]  Period, right panel: the elongation curves end at the same place, 1.18 for both. The model starts 8 percent high in absolute terms (0.0985 vs 0.091 s) but accumulates damage at the right rate. Tilt, left: peak tilt tracks the experiment to run 21 and reproduces the run-22 dip. Tilt, right: the one clear miss - both walls lean steadily from run 1 (that is the joist slip, 8-12 mm cumulative in the paper) while the model holds zero until run 18. With the pockets bonded, the model has no mechanism for that early drift. It catches the late positive swing though, and ends near the measured value.
